prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

The days are dog-eared, the edges torn, ragged—like those pages I ripped once out of library books, for their photos of Vallejo and bootless Robert Johnson. A fine needs paying now it’s true, but not by me. I am no more guilty than that thrush is who sits there stripping moss off the wet bark of a tree. A red fleck, like his, glows at the back of my head—a beauty mark, left by the brain’s after-jets. I would not wish for the three brains Robert required to double-clutch his guitar and chase those sounds he had to know led down and into a troubled dusky river, always. Three brains did Johnson no earthly good, neither his nor Vallejo’s 4 & 1/2 worked right exactly—O bunglers, O banged-up pans of disaster! Crying for days, said Cesar, & singing for months. How can I be so strong some times, at others weak? I wish to be free, but free to do what? To leave myself behind? To switch channels remotely? Better to sing. Not like the bird, but as they sang, Cesar & Robert— with the shocked & seeded sweetness of an apple split open by a meat cleaver.

The days are dog-eared, their edges torn and ragged—like the pages I once ripped from library books for their photographs of Vallejo and bootless Robert Johnson. A fine needs paying now, it’s true, but not by me. I am no more guilty than that thrush sitting there, stripping moss from the wet bark of a tree. A red fleck, like his, glows at the back of my head—a beauty mark left by the brain’s after-jets.

outputs.L2:
Time has become creased and frayed, its margins shredded, resembling the sheets I once tore from library volumes because they carried pictures of Vallejo and Robert Johnson without his boots. The overdue penalty must indeed be settled, though I will not be the one to settle it. My blame is no greater than that of the thrush perched nearby, peeling moss from rain-darkened tree bark. At the rear of my skull shines a crimson spot like the bird’s—a small ornament bestowed by the brain’s lingering exhaust.

I have no desire for the three minds Robert needed to shift his guitar’s gears twice over and pursue the music he surely understood would forever descend into a shadowed, turbulent river. Johnson gained no worldly advantage from those three brains; his did not function properly, nor did Vallejo’s four and a half. Oh, you fumblers, you battered vessels of catastrophe! César spoke of weeping for days and singing for months.

Why am I powerful at certain moments and frail at others? I long for freedom, but freedom for what purpose? To abandon who I am? To change the station from a distance? Singing would be wiser—not in the manner of the thrush, but as César and Robert sang: with the startled, seed-filled sweetness released when a butcher’s cleaver splits an apple apart.
outputs.L3:
The speaker compares their worn and ragged days to pages once torn from library books to obtain images of César Vallejo and Robert Johnson. This memory evokes both damage and devotion: the pages are mutilated, yet the act reflects a deep attachment to two admired artists. The speaker refuses to feel guilty for such acts, likening themself instead to an innocent thrush pulling moss from the wet bark of a tree—an instinctive creature taking what it needs without malice.

Yet the poem also hints at lasting injury. A red mark at the back of the speaker’s head suggests lingering physical or psychological damage, perhaps an aftereffect lodged in the brain. This vulnerability connects the speaker to Robert Johnson and Vallejo, both portrayed as brilliant but deeply troubled artists. Their extraordinary gifts did not shield them from pain, hardship, or uncertainty.

As the speaker’s strength rises and falls, freedom itself becomes difficult to define or trust. In response, the speaker does not seek purity, certainty, or escape. Instead, they conclude that it is better to sing in the manner of Johnson and Vallejo: with a wounded sweetness that transforms suffering into art.
outputs.L4:
The speaker moves through a fractured inner landscape shaped by guilt, memory, and a damaged consciousness. Rather than presenting suffering as a single, coherent experience, the poem renders it through broken images and abrupt allusions, suggesting a mind struggling to understand its own wounds. Freedom appears desirable but uncertain: the speaker longs to escape the burdens of the self, yet recognizes that no outward liberation can erase what has already been absorbed into consciousness.

The references to César Vallejo and Robert Johnson place this private anguish within a larger artistic tradition. Vallejo evokes poetry born from grief, isolation, and moral pain, while Johnson represents the blues artist who transforms suffering into music, even at the cost of being consumed by it. The thrush provides a natural counterpart to these figures. Its song does not deny injury or darkness; instead, it rises from within them, instinctive and exposed.

By bringing poet, bluesman, and bird together, the poem suggests that art is not an escape from suffering but a way of passing through it. The self cannot simply be abandoned, and guilt cannot be dissolved by imagining freedom. What remains possible is the act of singing: giving pain a rhythm, a voice, and a shape. The poem therefore ends with a difficult affirmation. Beauty is not presented as purity or consolation, but as something raw and wounded—a resilience created when the damaged self continues to speak.

**The Vallejo Legacy**

Robert Vallejo had always been fascinated by the stories hidden within his hometown—the old buildings, waterfront streets, and generations of families who had shaped the community. As a local historian, Robert collected photographs and personal accounts to preserve Vallejo’s changing identity.

His work showed that the city was more than a point on a map. For Robert, Vallejo represented resilience, cultural diversity, and the enduring connection between people and place.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about memory, guilt, and the desire for freedom, weaving together César Vallejo, blues guitarist Robert Johnson, a thrush stripping moss from a tree, and the aftermath of a brain injury.
counterfactuals.output:
After the blow, memory became a hotel with no stairs. I woke in its lobby each morning, holding a key stamped with yesterday’s number, while upstairs the furniture dragged itself from room to room. The doctors called this recovery. My mother called it mercy. César Vallejo sat beside the extinguished fountain, counting the bones in the rain. He said guilt is a coat sewn before birth: even naked, we feel its sleeves.

At dusk, Robert Johnson arrived with a guitar black as a closed road. He tuned it to the small electrical storms behind my eyes and played twelve bars for everything I could no longer name—the dog, the door, the face at the foot of the bed. Each note bent like a man confessing under a moon that refused to be a witness. I asked him where the crossroads were. He pointed to my skull.

Outside, a thrush stripped moss from a tree, green thread by green thread, exposing the pale bark beneath. It worked with the fierce patience of someone uncovering a crime. I watched through glass and felt the old guilt stir, though I could not remember what I had done. Perhaps guilt survives the evidence. Perhaps it is the last citizen of a ruined country, waving its flag over empty houses.

Vallejo began to weep for a Thursday that had not happened. Johnson laughed and slid a blue note under the locked door of my mind. The thrush flew off with its mouth full of softness.

Then the tree stood bare, almost free.

I wanted that bareness. I wanted the wind to pass through me without finding a hook, a name, a verdict. I wanted to walk beyond the crossroads, beyond the poem, beyond the bright machinery of the injured brain, where every forgotten thing waits in a field wearing my face.

But freedom, when it came, was not a gate. It was a bird returning for one more strand of moss. It was the guitar’s broken string still trembling. It was Vallejo placing his sorrow in my empty hand and saying: Carry nothing—yet carry this.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dense, lyrical monologue in which a speaker compares damaged days to torn library-book pages and reflects on Vallejo, Robert Johnson, neurological trauma, weakness, and singing as a form of survival.
counterfactuals.output:
Some days arrive already handled, already thumbed through by strangers, their margins greasy with weather, their corners worried soft; days torn from the library book of the body so that the sentence begins elsewhere and ends in a white wound. You can see the ragged fibers where Tuesday should have continued. You can feel the missing paragraph—someone walking into a room, someone lifting a cup, someone remembering his own name—but the page is gone, and the book has been returned through the night slot, stamped DAMAGED, though no one admits to having damaged it.

Vallejo knew the blows that come without genealogy, those black heralds with no country of origin. He stood under the arithmetic of rain and counted himself among the uncountable. I read him after the hospital, when language was a staircase with several steps removed, and every word had to leap its little gap of darkness. The neurologist called it trauma: a clean term, almost architectural, for the lightning-struck rooms behind my forehead, the wires frayed into sparks, the hand that forgot the cup while holding it. On the scans, injury flowered without fragrance. A pale weather. A country seen from above.

Weakness humiliated me at first. The spoon grew heavy. The hallway lengthened into history. My knees became two unreliable witnesses. I had believed the body was a servant who slept below stairs; then it stopped answering the bell, and I learned it had been the house, the stairs, the bell, the hand pulling the cord. Weakness was not emptiness but a fierce, crowded knowledge: each breath hauling its net, each finger negotiating with gravity, each morning assembling me from parts that no longer trusted the diagram.

And somewhere Robert Johnson bent a note until it confessed. Not at the crossroads of the legend—that is too tidy, too eager for a devil with paperwork—but at the crossroads inside the throat, where terror meets breath and breath, refusing extinction, becomes sound. His guitar carried the dry rattle of distance, the train leaving with one lamp burning, the dog of loneliness scratching at the door. He sang as if pursued, yes, but also as if pursuit itself could be given rhythm, made to keep time, made for three minutes to obey.

That is what I began to understand: singing does not heal the torn page. It does not restore the lost noun, resurrect the afternoon, persuade the nerve to carry its blue message cleanly. Singing threads the tear with air. It says: here is the place the text was taken; here is the mouth-shaped absence; here, nevertheless, the story crosses.

So I sing badly. I sing with the cracked instrument I was issued after impact. I sing Vallejo’s impossible Thursday, Johnson’s road dissolving under moonlight, the clinical words—lesion, tremor, deficit—until they lose their white coats and kneel among the human noises. I sing when my voice is only a match failing in rain. I sing because weakness has its register, low and stubborn, and because the damaged brain, that burned library, still shelters a few books whose pages flutter when the lungs open.

Listen: the torn days are not silent. Put your ear to the ragged edge. The missing paper whispers through what remains. Even the blank has grain; even ruin remembers the tree. I cannot return the book unmarked. I cannot pay the fine with sorrow. But I can stand at the desk of morning, shaking, and read aloud from the fragments. I can make breath carry what memory drops. I can sing—not to prove I survived, but to survive the next note, and the next, until the song, wounded and unfinished, carries me beyond the sentence that broke.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental prose poem with ragged punctuation, ampersands, startling metaphors, and dark humor. Include stolen photographs from library books, a red mark at the back of the speaker’s head, multiple brains, a troubled river, and an apple split by a meat cleaver.
counterfactuals.output:
I keep stolen photographs from library books  
under my tongue—  
dead astronomers, bridges with their mouths open,  
a woman in 1912 holding a pear  
as if gravity were a small obedient dog.

At the back of my head: a red mark.  
Not wound, exactly. More like punctuation  
the body forgot to explain—  
an asterisk leading nowhere *

& the doctor says I have multiple brains.  
One for weather. One for debt. One  
keeps phoning the dead & hanging up.  
The smallest wears a paper crown,  
calls itself Management.

Outside, the river is troubled again—  
dragging its long wet sentence through town,  
arguing with pylons, swallowing streetlamps.  
We send it a card:  
GET WELL / OR ELSE.

In the kitchen an apple waits  
on the block, green as envy’s little planet.  
I raise the meat cleaver—

                           thock.

Two white rooms.  
A few black seeds.  
No scream, which is frankly unprofessional.

I photograph the halves & paste them  
into a book about mercy.  
The librarian stamps my wrist  
DUE BACK NEVER.

Behind my eyes, the brains applaud  
with all their tiny, frightened hands;  
the river coughs up a shoe;  
the red mark burns like an exit sign—

& I go on living,  
that old dark joke  
with no punchline  
but excellent circulation.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Imagine a brain-injured narrator watching a thrush on wet bark while meditating on artistic genius and suffering. Have them invoke César Vallejo and Robert Johnson, question what freedom means, and conclude that it is better to sing.
counterfactuals.output:
The thrush grips the wet bark as if the world were tilting. Perhaps it is. Since the injury, straight lines lean toward me; light arrives with a bruise around it. The doctors call this damage. I call it weather.

The bird cocks its head, listening for what moves beneath the bark. I think of César Vallejo, who knew that sorrow could be made to stammer until it became music. I think of Robert Johnson at the crossroads, trading—so the story says—whatever a man owns for the power to make pain answer in another key.

Is that genius: suffering taught to sing? Or is that merely the consolation of those who survive the song?

Freedom, then—what is it? To escape the wound? To choose it? To refuse the names others give it? My mind cannot cross a room without losing something, yet the thrush opens its throat in the rain as if nothing has ever been taken from it.

The bark shines black. The morning trembles. I do not know whether we are free.

But it is better to sing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a single-paragraph literary passage in a fragmented, hallucinatory voice about damaged consciousness. Blend blues mythology, Latin American poetry, guilt over defaced library books, channel-switching imagery, and the contrast between birdsong and human art.
counterfactuals.output: At three in the morning the crossroads tuned itself between stations, one channel snowing blue fire, another showing a black dog asleep beneath the gallows of the moon, and through both of them the singer walked backward, guitar full of rain, his shadow already sold. I had been tearing faces from library books—saints, dictators, women with rivers in their hair—and now every margin accused me in small penciled voices: thief, orphan, butcher of borrowed worlds. Somewhere south of sleep, Neruda’s salt was rusting on the windowsill, Vallejo’s stones were learning my name, and the television kept changing without a hand: war, soap opera, sermon, a field of sugarcane bending under invisible breath. My mind came apart politely, page by page, while outside a thrush poured one clean phrase into the ruined dawn, effortless and unashamed. We answered with paintings, requiems, guitars strung with wire and grief; we built museums around the wound. The bird repeated itself and made no monument. Then the screen went black, and in it I saw my face crossed out, overdue, singing the blues to a library that had burned years ago.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
